one_liner: Pure-Java PNG encoder that beats javax.imageio's PNG writer by compressing image segments in parallel on a thread pool.
what_it_does: Encodes a java.awt.image.BufferedImage to PNG (8- and 16-bit RGB, ARGB, grayscale and indexed) through a small immutable builder: new PngEncoder().withBufferedImage(img).withCompressionLevel(n).toStream/toFile/toBytes(). It replaces ImageIO.write(img, "png", out) for writing only; there is no decoder and almost no metadata support (no text chunks), though ICC profiles, sRGB/gAMA/cHRM and pHYs chunks can be written. Published on Maven Central as com.pngencoder:pngencoder (0.16.0), MIT licensed.
how_it_is_fast: The speedup is mostly parallel DEFLATE: scanlines are cut into segments of at least 128 KiB (raw size / (9 x availableProcessors)), each segment is compressed by a thread-local raw java.util.zip.Deflater with SYNC_FLUSH on a shared fixed pool of availableProcessors daemon threads, and the byte-aligned outputs are concatenated with a combined Adler-32, in the style of pigz. Each segment starts with an empty dictionary, which costs about 2% in size. By default it also skips PNG row filtering (filter type 0 on every row), whereas ImageIO tries all five filters per row; scanlines are pulled straight from the raster's int/byte buffer for the common BufferedImage types, and Deflater objects are reused per thread.
when_to_use: A JVM service or batch job that writes large PNGs (multi-megapixel photos, renders, screenshots) on a machine with several idle cores and no JNI allowed.
Latency of a single large encode matters more than total CPU spent, e.g. one request thread producing one big image while other cores are free.
You want a dependency-free, Java 8 compatible ImageIO replacement with a tunable compression level (level 1 trades about 2.5x larger files for about 2.3x more speed per the README table).
Images known to have at most 256 colors, where withTryIndexedEncoding(true) plus withPredictorEncoding(true) gives smaller files than ImageIO (at extra time).
when_not_to_use: Servers already encoding many images concurrently: the pool is one static fixed pool of availableProcessors threads shared by all callers, so the parallel gain mostly disappears (the project's own 8-thread JMH runner commit is titled 'ImageIO gains more :(' and publishes no numbers).

Single-core or CPU-limited containers: the README says the speedup will not be significant there, and an independent single-threaded JMH run (FPNG-Java suite, JDK 21) measured only 1.13x to 1.44x over ImageIO even at compression level 2.
Small images: when the raw scanline data is at most one segment (128 KiB, about 181x181 RGBA, derived from code) it always encodes on the calling thread with a plain Deflater.

When smallest output matters at default settings: unfiltered rows compress worse than ImageIO's adaptive filtering on photographic content, so you must enable predictor encoding and give back much of the speed.

When you need much higher throughput and JNI is acceptable: native fpng (SSE2) and fpnge (AVX2) through the FPNG-Java wrapper took about 4x to 20x less time than PngEncoder at level 2 in that same JDK 21 suite (derived from page data).

integration.dependencies: none (JDK java.awt and java.util.zip only; JUnit, Hamcrest and JMH are test-scope)
integration.min_toolchain: Java 8 (maven.compiler.source/target 8); no module-info (issue #59 open; PR #124 for Automatic-Module-Name is unmerged)
integration.platforms: any JVM with java.desktop/AWT image classes
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the code shows immutable builder objects, thread-local Deflaters and per-call buffer pools, so concurrent calls look safe, but all calls share one static fixed thread pool sized at class-load time and the calling thread blocks while its segments compress.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces ImageIO.write(img, "png", ...) only; different API, no ImageWriteParam/IIOMetadata support, encoder only

gotchas: Default output is unfiltered and split into independent deflate segments, so files are not byte-identical to ImageIO and are typically somewhat larger; the 'about the same size as ImageIO' claim was never measured by the benchmark, and ImageIO itself uses deflate level 9 on JDK 8 but level 4 on JDK 9+.

Peak transient memory in multithreaded mode is roughly 0.75x the raw scanline size on top of the image: up to 3 x availableProcessors queued segments, each holding two pool buffers of 1.125x the segment size (derived from PngEncoderDeflaterOutputStream and PngEncoderDeflaterBufferPool). That is about 90 MB for a 4900x6000 RGBA image.

toStream()/toFile() return a byte count that omits the sRGB, gAMA, cHRM, pHYs, iCCP, PLTE and tRNS chunks, because PngEncoderLogic.encode writes those to the raw stream instead of its counting wrapper; do not use the return value as the file size when those chunks are present.

The test helper PngEncoderTestUtil.assertThatPixelIs computes alphaExpected from the actual pixel, so round-trip tests accept any pixel whose decoded alpha is 0; an earlier indexed-encoding corruption bug (issue #34) was fixed in 2022.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you must stay pure Java on the JVM; mtpng and pngenc use the same parallel-deflate idea natively (Rust with a C API, and C), and fpng/fpnge are far faster but need native code and give larger files on big photos.
verified_claims_summary: First-party JMH (1 fork, one 5 s measurement iteration, one benchmark thread, CPU and JDK not stated, '8 logical cores'): PngEncoder at level 9, unfiltered, compressing on an 8-thread pool encoded 5.1x to 7.1x more images per second than single-threaded ImageIO.write with defaults (random 1024x1024 ARGB, a 2121x350 logo, a 4900x6000 photo). An independent JMH suite in manticore-projects/FPNG-Java (JDK 21.0.1 GraalVM CE, -XX:+UseSerialGC, 10 iterations, CPU not stated) ran pngencoder 0.14.0 with multithreading disabled: at level 2 it took 0.70 to 0.88 of ImageIO's time (1.13x to 1.44x faster; 1120 vs 1270 ms on the same 4900x6000 photo) and at level 1 it was 2.26x to 3.53x faster (derived from page data), with output sizes not shown in the README.
status_note: Active but in maintenance mode (last commit 2025-11-25, release 0.16.0 of 2025-05-19, later commits are dependency bumps); MIT licensed, Java 8, no dependencies and small enough to vendor.
measurement_notes: Independent measurement found: the manticore-projects/FPNG-Java README publishes a JMH table (JMH 1.37, JDK 21.0.1 GraalVM CE 23.1, -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xms512M -Xmx2G, avgt, 10 samples with error bars; CPU not stated) whose PNGEncoderBenchmark.java calls com.pngencoder 0.14.0 with withMultiThreadedCompressionEnabled(false). At withCompressionLevel(2) it took 1120.410 ms against ImageIO's 1270.494 ms on looklet-look-scale6.png (the same 4900x6000 photo as the first-party table), 4 channels (1.13x), 854.307 vs 1099.045 ms with 3 channels (1.29x), and 44.704 vs 64.538 ms and 39.813 vs 54.189 ms on example.png (1.44x and 1.36x). At level 1 the ratios are 2.97x, 3.53x, 2.29x and 2.26x (all derived from page data). ImageIO there is JDK 21's writer (deflate level 4 plus adaptive filtering, confirmed in openjdk PNGImageWriter.java and RowFilter.java), writing to a ByteArrayOutputStream. Output sizes are said to be in a benchmark.ods that returned 404. The table shows a 'channels' parameter that the current EncoderBenchmark.java does not define, and 10 samples where build.gradle sets 3 iterations, so it came from an earlier harness revision. This independent single-threaded figure supports the verifier's reading that the README's 5.1x-7.1x comes mainly from the 8-thread pool. In the first-party table, the random 1024x1024 ARGB case (7.1x) is incompressible noise, where ImageIO's five-filter trial per row is pure overhead. Code defects found that do not affect the published numbers: toStream()/toFile() undercount the returned byte size when ancillary chunks are written; PngEncoderTestUtil.assertThatPixelIs uses actual for alphaExpected; getProfileName's UTF-16 branch reads data[endIdx] twice instead of data[endIdx+1]. The README's example comment says level 1 is 'about three times faster' with files 'about three times larger', while its own table says 2.31x speed and 2.50x size.
